en: No one could endure him.
They grappled and clashed,
Fought and spilled blood.
War horns and trumpets sounded;
That frenzied champion, eager for strife,
Had the muskets fire in need.
A vast, rending tumult arose,
And his monstrous excess became plain.
He donned his bulletproof armor.
“He is an unbearably mighty champion,” they said;
“He has become death itself,” they said;
“Those who go against him never return,” they said.
His people lamented and the nation cried out,
Despairing of their own lives.
The strange wrath of that swine
Revealed his monstrous savagery.
Such was Sarybai’s nature.
When roused, he went berserk,
Like the long ridge of Kaptal-Too.
When wrathfully enraged,
He was like a vast expanse of Kök-Ap.
When they saw Sarybai,
Warriors despaired of life.
He bore an iron spear,
And a steel mace was fastened upon him.
Sparks blazed from his mace;
When he opened his mouth, fire burned—
He seemed to blaze unnaturally.
When one considers God the Creator,
He fashioned every manner of living soul.
His saddle’s forebow hung down
Like a grain merchant’s sack.
The breath issuing from his mouth
Was like flame from a forge.
His brow was high, his venom fierce;
Such was his appearance to the eye.
He drove his splendid army onward,
Driving the whole host together.
Anyone who watched carefully
Despaired of his entrusted life.
Misery seethed across the wide world;
A red haze of dust rose.
The land spread wondrously before the eye.
That infidel, son of a demon swine,
Raised seven sacred banners
And stirred seventy separate tumults.
Dark-bladed spears swayed,
And black-iron Zulfikar swords
Flashed in every hand.
Their patterns divided into countless ranks;
They looked like giants and demons.
Mounted on camels, they carried spears—
What kind of beings were these, cursed to strike from above?
He truly had a champion army,
A fearsome force assembled.
It was massed like blue steel.
How could this stone-hearted one’s aspect
Be so imposing?
He sated the bold with battle,
Dividing all this host without remainder.
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
Look upon the army he commanded:
Sturdy-limbed, hulking brutes.
At the word “Go!” they closed in;
Every soul they hunted submitted.
Their forms were unlike those of men.
When a mortal dared confront them,
Heedless of person or people,
They blazed their Venus-bright eyes,
And made human misery seethe.
They had their hour of drinking blood—
A truly formidable host had assembled.
Among that hollow-chested horde,
In the absence of the daughter of Kaiypchal,
They took the lead in the battle.
Külchoro and brave Seytek,
Together with lionhearted Semetey,
Fought until the grass ripened and swayed,
Until the meadow flowers scattered;
Until every ravine and gorge
Was filled with bristling white snow;
Until the wind whistled down every valley
And drove the dust before it;
Until the birches shed their ashen leaves,
And the rowans lost their buds;
Until the flowering trees withered,
Autumn waned and winter came,
The feather grass dried and reeds grew old,
Until seven full months had passed.
No single warrior remained without a wounded horse,
No brow remained unbroken,
No forehead remained unscarred.
They stood face-to-face,
With the lionlike champion,
With the warrior named Semetey.
Divine Shay upheld Külchoro,
And the dashing warrior Seytek;
For seven full months they fought.
Banners fell and khans died;
Every soul who clashed in battle died.
Through seventy days of fighting,
The seasoned gray-wolf warrior,
Wounded in seven places,
Stooped with his back bent,
His eyes bulging and blazing,
Gathered all his remaining strength.
Though they fought, they could not prevail;
They could not defeat that mighty brute.
All the people were slaughtered.
Külchoro mustered his courage,
Semetey joined the clash,
And hero Seytek shattered the ranks.
Champion of every living soul,
Wisdom of all who lived,
Strongman of all mankind,
The morning star of Bagdagül.
Many heroes fell to bullets;
Such was the conflict and turmoil.
When they clashed, none could prevail against them—
Descendants of the honored lion,
Offshoots of pure steel,
Who destroyed all they encountered,
Descendants of the cherished hero.
Their first forefather was Tügöl Khan;
That gray wolf of ancient roots
Had made eighty-four charges,
And every charge he made was fire.
Enemies who came against him met destruction;
He was a born lion.
He was the fortress of the white-capped Kyrgyz;
Never, it was said, would another such soul be born.
Just behold how the son
Surpassed his father!
No mortal had ever faced him;
No enemy, however fiercely resolved,
Had defeated him in battle.
Descendant of the commanding lion,
He would not yield even to ten men.
God had prospered his deeds.
He was nothing like Sarybai,
Who ravaged nations and slaughtered peoples.
His arms filled with strength;
Those he grappled fell and lay level with the earth.
Struck by an unseen power,
The cherished warrior gained strength,
And all the men who grappled with him
He scattered, spilling their blood.
He had grown fierce from destroying foes;
The son, surpassing his father,
Came to be called a lion.
He fought with Sarybai,
Standing against him on the battlefield.
They faced each other and fought
Until their strength was exhausted.
Akolpok, which no spear could pierce,
Was torn apart like scattered ash.
The troops cried out and recoiled.
Sable mail with lark-eye links,
With a jewel-studded collar and copper sleeves,
And costly crimson
Bulletproof coats were shredded.
Many champions and many lions,
Mighty, wise strongmen—
So many heroes were slaughtered.
So many conflicts had occurred;
So many heroes and lionhearts
Had been swallowed by the swine Sarybai.
They struck but could not prevail;
They could not defeat the son of Zhelmoguz.
The fierce champions and lionhearted warriors who came
Fought but could not defeat him.
They clutched their collars in grief,
Despairing of their fly-sized lives.
The overturning world’s
Deceit became plain.
They stood face-to-face,
Having ridden out to single combat.
The three fierce warriors, one after another,
Fought him in turn.
On the great battlefield where the people suffered,
In a deserted ravine where no living soul passed,
Stood noble gray-wolf Semetey,
Külchoro on his Karala,
The spring of the hill country,
Brave Seytek, born after his father’s death,
Semetey’s valiant son.
They stood face-to-face,
Shouting as they thrust their spears,
Until strength failed and power departed,
Fighting day and night.
Who had ever seen such a deed?
The two arms that had served them
Were paralyzed and could no longer rise.
Their precious heads, needed while alive,
Were drenched like crimson buckets of blood.
Their precious lives, alluring to those doomed to die,
Longed for a single glimpse of deliverance.
Unable to overcome Sarybai,
Each day they endured felt bound to a span.
Death, from which no traveler returns,
Circled close before their brows.
Their bulletproof coats of armor were pierced,
Their many layers falling away,
Every lining torn loose.
They fought but could not prevail.
That infidel son of Zhelmoguz
Kept demanding battle in this way.
The one destined to grapple with him was Kuyaly,
The champion maiden who would oppose him.
She took the cast-iron-headed weapon in hand.
At the very sight of the hero Sarybai,
Take fright and flee far away!
Unable to prevail in combat,
Those golden heads suffered torment.
He turned toward the battlefield,
And raised in his hand
The steel-hafted battle-axe.
With a ringing clang, utterly unconcerned,
He vowed to break the banner
Of Manas’s heroic descendants and slaughter them,
To wipe out their entire line.
The champion warriors who clashed with him,
The lions upheld by divine Shay,
He valued no more than his boot heels.
Strength and valor, sport and battlecraft—
God Almighty had granted that swine
Without measure.
True champions and lionhearted warriors
He valued no more than a belt-string.
He neither swerved nor flinched,
Neither faltered nor stirred,
But stood like a forest lion.
He seemed to trample the eighteen thousand worlds
Underfoot like kneaded dough.
When he appeared in all his menace,
He resembled a deep-dug grave.
The infidel’s roaring
Was like a flood bursting from a mountainside.
He rumbled and worked himself into a fury,
Muttering to himself.
His shape shifted strangely;
He seemed ancient-rooted and immovable.
Wits were confounded and hands went numb,
All order overturned and broke apart.
When he charged in wrath,
Setting his threatening gaze and lunging,
He was like a craggy mountain ridge.
The eighteen thousand worlds—
Not merely the world, but every beast,
Every living creature—
He seemed born to drive and crush.
The lower realm was thick and vast,
Yet when the infidel showed his menace,
He seemed able to burst through its very depths.
Every creature that moved
He seemed ready to slaughter and devour,
